title: SAP Lead Assessment Rubric
purpose: Score a 60-90 second architecture or process answer. Reward problem framing, contradiction thinking, options, authority design, evidence and concise Lead communication.

anchors.0: Jumps directly to a product, transaction or configuration change.
anchors.1: Restates the symptom but not the business outcome or affected object.
anchors.2: Names the business outcome and main actors, but boundary or evidence is weak.
anchors.3: Frames observed behavior, useful function, business object, boundary and key evidence.
anchors.4: Also separates facts, assumptions and constraints, and identifies the decision that matters.

anchors.1: Names a generic trade-off where one side is obviously undesirable.
anchors.2: Names two useful properties but accepts compromise too early.
anchors.3: States why both sides are useful and selects a plausible separation operator.
anchors.4: Tests more than one separation axis and shows how the conflict can disappear for different conditions, times, contexts, levels, authorities or representations.

anchors.1: Offers several products that implement the same design.
anchors.2: Offers two technical alternatives with limited process or ownership change.
anchors.3: Offers at least two materially different system shapes with trade-offs.
anchors.4: Includes simplification, deterministic redesign and uncertainty-assisted design where relevant, and states the complexity tax of each.

anchors.0: Technology choice and authority are mixed together or uncontrolled.
anchors.1: Mentions controls but ownership is vague.
anchors.2: Separates some deterministic rules from flexible logic.
anchors.3: Places rules, workflow, events, retrieval, AI and human judgment deliberately and names accountable ownership.
anchors.4: Also separates read, propose, validate, approve and execute, with risk-based limits and reversibility.

anchors.0: No evidence or test is proposed.
anchors.2: Names useful evidence and a primary metric.
anchors.3: Adds a counter-metric and a bounded test scope.
anchors.4: Adds failure condition, rollback or recovery, and explains what evidence would change the recommendation.

anchors.0: Answer is a list of features or acronyms.
anchors.1: Technically correct but difficult to follow.
anchors.2: Has a clear recommendation but weak structure or ownership language.
anchors.3: Concise structure: problem, contradiction, options, decision criteria, experiment.
anchors.4: Makes uncertainty explicit, avoids false certainty, and explains the decision in business and architecture language within 60-90 seconds.

bands.name: Narrow solution answer
bands.interpretation: Mostly configuration or product thinking. Needs stronger business framing and system trade-offs.

bands.name: Solid consultant answer
bands.interpretation: Good delivery knowledge, but the architecture decision and counter-effects are not yet consistently explicit.

bands.name: Lead-ready answer
bands.interpretation: Frames the problem, exposes trade-offs, compares system shapes and links the recommendation to evidence and ownership.

bands.name: Strong Lead answer
bands.interpretation: Shows system-level judgment, authority design, reversible experimentation and concise communication without pretending uncertainty is gone.

hard_fail_signals.label: Vendor or product selected before problem and boundary are clear
Only one system shape is considered
No accountable owner or write/approval boundary
AI capability is treated as authorization
Only the improvement metric is measured
Current configuration, policy or system behavior is invented instead of marked unknown

answer_spine: Frame the observed behavior and useful function.
State the contradiction: improving A makes useful property B worse.
Separate the conflict by condition, time, context, level, authority or representation.
Compare at least two materially different system shapes.
Allocate deterministic logic, workflow/events, AI and human authority deliberately.
Name the evidence, experiment, primary metric and counter-metric.
